| [NOTE-052](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-052.md) v2 | Consciousness in AI: indicator properties | The report assumes computational functionalism and takes a "theory-heavy" approach. From it the authors derive 14 indicator properties: RPT-1–2, GWT-1–4, HOT-1–4, AST-1, PP-1 and AE-1–2. The claim for them is only that more of them raises the probability of consciousness. They assess a handful of systems against subsets of the list and conclude that no current system "appears to be a strong candidate". Transformer LLMs have "only a relatively weak case" for any GWT indicator, because a single forward pass has no recurrence or global broadcast. | [NOTE-089](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-089.md) | Nagel: what is it like to be a bat | An organism is conscious if and only if there is something it is like to be it. That subjective character is tied to a type of point of view. Every functional, intentional or causal-role analysis leaves it out, since each is compatible with its absence. Psychophysical reduction therefore cannot follow the usual pattern of dropping a point of view in favour of a more objective description of the same thing: for experience, that leads away from the phenomenon. Physicalism is left not refuted but not yet understandable. The closing proposal is an "objective phenomenology" of the structure of experience. | Read |

| [NOTE-122](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-122.md) v2 | Barrett et al. — IIT: good, bad and misunderstood | A position paper with no new formal result. It argues four things. IIT's algorithm is undefined whenever any spatial, temporal or state graining of a system is non-Markovian (Barrett & Mediano 2019), and so gives no output for brains; it cannot handle unbounded continuous state variables; and it has never been computed on any real system. | [NOTE-131](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-131.md) v2 | Schwitzgebel — If materialism is true, the US is conscious | A conditional, informal argument. Any materialist criterion liberal enough to credit rabbits (and rabbit-level distributed aliens, the "squidbits") and behaviourally human-like but oddly built aliens (Sirian supersquids, Antarean antheads) with consciousness also credits the United States. On this argument the US meets the usual materialist marks of consciousness: sophisticated information processing (roughly 10^14 person-to-person visual "connections", comparable to the brain's about 10^14 synapses), goal-directed environmental responsiveness, self-representation and historical embedding. The only exits are eliminativism, extreme sparseness or neurochauvinism, each costlier than the conclusion. The paper argues for no universal criterion. It ends undecided between three readings: US consciousness, a challenge to materialists, or grounds to distrust universal metaphysics of mind. | Read |
| [NOTE-135](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-135.md) v2 | Kleiner & Ludwig — Mathematical structure of experience | The paper proposes a definition, (MSC). A mathematical structure S = ((A_i), (S_j)) is a structure *of* conscious experience iff (S1) its domains are sets of experiential aspects, and (S2) every relation or function S_j has an "S_j-aspect". An S_j-aspect is an aspect that a variation of experience changes exactly when the variation fails to preserve S_j. The older condition (MDC), that a structure is "of" experience if its domains are aspects and its axioms hold, survives only as the necessary condition for *describing* experience, because as a sufficient condition it admits incompatible structures (discrete and non-discrete topologies on the same set), arbitrary re-definitions (every C·d for C > 0) and consciousness-indifferent structures. Worked examples: experienced relative similarity is a strict partial order that satisfies (MSC), given transitivity (assumed). Visual regions form a topology that satisfies (MSC), given Bayne and Chalmers's subsumptive unity thesis. | Read |

| [NOTE-143](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-143.md) v2 | Frankish — Closing the Cartesian Bureau de Change | An illusionist's commentary on Veit's *A Philosophy for the Science of Animal Consciousness*. Frankish places Veit's function-first, evolutionary programme in a "post-Cartesian" (qualia-eliminativist) paradigm. He then argues that two things drag it back towards Cartesianism: Veit keeps the words "qualia" and "phenomenal", and he writes as if hedonic valence motivates action "in virtue of its feel". | [NOTE-146](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-146.md) v2 | Winkielman et al. — The coherent and fluent mind | An opinion piece proposing an extra route to the unity of consciousness across the senses. | [NOTE-187](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-187.md) | On the Evolution, Science, and Metaphysics of Consciousness | Veit's reply to five commentaries on *A Philosophy for the Science of Animal Consciousness* (2023). Its main new content is the metaphysics the book left to one paragraph. He says hedonic "feel" is *identical* with a valence system: "a common currency of sharing evaluative information across multiple control systems". The currency metaphor, he says, is "not Cartesian but cybernetic" (p. 10). He keeps the word "qualia", arguing that Cartesians have no "definitional rights" (p. 9), and he insists the pathological complexity thesis (PCT) is compatible with any metaphysics, dualism and panpsychism included (p. 9). Against his other critics, he defends a bottom-up evolutionary method that uses human data (de Weerd); a naturalism that is neither autopoietic nor biopsychist (Sachs); evaluation-first over prediction-first, consciousness as an adaptation, and graded, partial unity (Suzuki); and the link to welfare science (Chincarini). | Read |
| [NOTE-188](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-188.md) | The Weirdness of the World | The book's thesis is that every viable theory of how consciousness fits into the cosmos, and of the cosmos's basic structure, is both "bizarre" (contrary to common sense) and "dubious" (not rationally compelling). So "something that seems almost too crazy to believe must be true" (p. 4), and credence should be spread across the bizarre options. Examples of those options are that the United States is conscious (if materialism is true), that we are sims or Boltzmann brains (a 0.1–1% credence), that space is transcendentally ideal, that almost every act causes almost every future event, and that there is no fact about snail consciousness. Its only positive empirical results are three self-experiments against solipsism (for example, 17 of 19 decisive chess games lost, p < .001). Everything else is informal argument. | Read |
